It’s been going on for at least a year, but in the last six months it’s completely taken over my life.

I’m constantly convinced there’s something seriously wrong with my body. It starts with something tiny—like a twitch in my calf or a bit of indigestion—and my brain just locks onto it. Within minutes I’m spiraling: “What if it’s cancer? What if it’s some rare disease?” I’ll reread the same lab results over and over, refresh health websites, search symptoms late into the night. Even when a doctor says I’m fine, it only calms me for a day or two before I find a new “sign” that something’s wrong.

At the same time, I’ve developed these rituals with my workspace and apartment. My desk, the whiteboard, even the mugs in the kitchen have to be lined up in a very exact way—angles, spacing, color order. If something’s off, I can’t focus on investor calls or product work until I fix it, sometimes for an hour or more. The team thinks I’m just “detail-oriented,” but it’s killing my productivity. The company’s collapsing and I’m stuck rearranging pens and checking my pulse.
